definition: Forage means to search around for food.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word forage. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know forage should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Black bears forage almost around the clock in late September, laying on the fat that will carry them through the den months.
Grazing asks no search at all — the meal is the field underfoot, eaten where the animal stands — while to forage is to go looking, because nothing is waiting underfoot.
Scavenge goes past forage — the forager seeks out food where it grows; the scavenger lives on scraps, refuse, and whatever something else left behind.

To rummage is the same rooting around moved indoors — through drawers, bins, and glove boxes — and food is beside the point. To forage is to search the outdoors for something to eat: the two verbs share the hunting posture, but only forage puts a meal at the end.

To glean is to gather what a harvest left behind — dropped ears of grain, missed apples — one narrow and tidy kind of food-searching. To forage is the wider verb: hunting out food wherever it grows wild, with no harvest required and no field to follow.

The mushroom club's autumn walk has two rules and one ritual.
Rule one: nothing goes in your basket until a guide has named it twice.
Rule two: cut, don't pull, so the ground keeps its secret for next year.
The ritual comes at noon, when forty people who have spent the morning foraging under the pines compare baskets — and the retired pharmacist, as always, has quietly out-gathered everyone.
Forage is the exact word for what they are doing, because it means to search around for food — the looking is the heart of it.
Nobody planted these chanterelles and no shelf holds them; the meal has to be found, patch by patch, which is why the verb belongs equally to bears in September and to people with baskets.
Forage is the naturalist's everyday verb, equally at home with bears, hens, and humans with baskets — the emphasis is always on searching.
Keep it apart from this unit's migrate, which is about moving between regions, not hunting a meal: a herd migrates to the winter range, and then it forages there.
For rooting through a junk drawer, rummage is the word; forage without food in view is a joke, and usually told as one.

A honeybee colony runs on the work of its oldest daughters.
In the last weeks of their lives, workers leave the hive to forage, flying as far as five miles in search of nectar and pollen.
A returning worker performs a waggle dance on the comb, its angle and length telling her sisters where the best flowers wait.
Researchers who tagged thousands of bees found that a strong hive can mount tens of thousands of such flights in a day.
The colony eats only what those flights bring back — a life staked, from first light on, on hunting down its food.
